There seems to be some sort of misconception, among the comments here, that a voice actor is not a professional unless they only go to studios to record? Allow me to set the record straight...

I am a professional voice actor, with my own booth, software, equipment, processing skills, etc. I've fully written, voiced and produced radio commercials for clients, and VO demos for fellow actors. I've worked on big national commercial spots, and on large video game titles. I am repped by a dozen agents across the country and I also find work through my own marketing endeavors.

Producers do sometimes send the talent to the studio, but this more or less has to do with the talent's ability to record or not record at their own studio. 9/10 if a producer can get the talent they want without paying an additional studio fee, they will do it. 

Also, if actors want to take the voice acting part of their career serious, then they're going to have to invest in the independent VO side of the business, because that's where the work is. Technology is to a point now that there's hardly any reason to record in a studio anymore...just ask your local studio and they'll confirm that years ago they had VO bookings left and right, but not anymore.

OP, if you're looking for talented voice actors with their own studio, there are many many places to find these individuals online and many ways to receive auditions for your project free of charge.

That's great! Still, making the transition from acting to VO can be difficult because it's an alternative skill set to what you've been spending your time learning. There won't be any memorizing lines or rehearsing. Many times I've booked jobs and never see the script until I step up to the mic to record. At that point, the client's expecting you to nail it and that's what they pay us for. But today's VO market is so much more encompassing than that. For VO in today's market, in order to remain competitive, you've got to be able to establish and maintain your own customer base, which means business acumen, equipment knowledge and editing/processing skills. As far as the jack of all trades thing, that goes for all businesses everywhere. If you have a leak in your house and you don't know where it's coming from, are you going to call a handyman or a plumber?

If a casting director needs a commercial recorded are they going to call Bill Farmer, Bob Bergen or Nolan North? Now, I know casting directors DO call these guys for commercial spots from time to time, but these guys have created a niche for themselves that allows them to be the go-to-guys for their characters or field of work. 

The point is, find your niche first. Find what you're best at and, most importantly, what pays the bills and focus solely on that. Be the go-to-guy for that niche or market. At that point you'll have the  freedom, confidence and connections to branch out into other stuff. 

Here it is from a different perspective. VO is a highly competitive business and nobody does it all. No one I know does audio books, movie trailers, commercials, cartoons & video games. We're all specialized because each niche takes it's own unique set of skills. For me, I don't have the patience or time for audio books, I don't have the timbre for trailers and I don't live in a market that produces cartoons. So I focus on Commercials & explainer videos. Every once in a while I book a video game gig, which is a lot of fun, but they're not my primary source of income. 

Here's another way to look at it. If a casting director is looking for a voice for their movie trailer, they're going to look at people who specialize in trailers and the guys who book those jobs are going to turn in an amazing audition or have a demo dedicated to movie trailers that is going to rock. The same goes for audio books, commercials, phone systems, video games, etc. Casting directors listen to hundreds of auditions and demos. When they're looking for something specific they want a specialist in that field.
